steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on detecting text generated by large language models and attributing it to its source model, focused on a cross-model detection setting studied across many model sizes and families. Motivate the problem, explain the setting and what makes the study comprehensive, and end with a contributions list and a pointer to the rest of the paper.

steps.text:
- LLMs, their uses, and concerns about misuse; need for detection and attribution
- Motivation: unknown source model -> Cross-Model Detection
- Comprehensiveness of the study
- What the broad study lets us learn
- Contributions
- Roadmap of the paper

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate text that is human-like, and they are used in many domains, for example content generation, chatbots and language translation. But as LLMs are used more and more, there are concerns about their misuse, about misinformation and about ethical implications. One way to address these concerns is to have robust methods that can detect and attribute text that was generated by LLMs, so that we can tell human-authored content apart from machine-generated content, identify the model that produced it, or even the model creator. These capabilities are crucial for keeping trust in online communication platforms, for content moderation, and for making sure AI is deployed responsibly.

The motivation for this research comes from real-life scenarios, where we often do not know which specific model was used to generate a piece of text. We can formulate these scenarios as "Cross-Model Detection". Here we look at whether a classifier that was trained to distinguish text generated by one LM from human-written text can also identify text that was generated by a different LM, without fine-tuning or training on the text that this other LM produces.

- Comprehensiveness
  - previous works: only a few model sizes and families
  - we: wide range of LLM sizes, base to exceptionally large; GPT-2, LLaMA, Pythia, OPT and others
  - conversational fine-tuning (Chat, Instruct, RLHF), quantization, watermarking -> effect on generalization/transferability
- What it lets us learn
  - deeper understanding of generalization/transferability; removes potential bias
  - impact of size, family, conversational finetuning, quantization, watermarking on detection and attribution
- Contributions
  - comprehensive cross-model detection + attribution study
  - size and family: inverse relationship effectiveness vs size; training on similar sizes helps; detection robust to finetuning, quantization, watermarking
  - attribution: human text distinguishable; confusion within family / adjacent sizes; distinct signatures
- Roadmap: related work, methodology, experiments, results

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate text that is human-like, and they are used in many domains, for example content generation, chatbots and language translation. But as LLMs are used more and more, there are concerns about their misuse, about misinformation and about ethical implications. One way to address these concerns is to have robust methods that can detect and attribute text that was generated by LLMs, so that we can tell human-authored content apart from machine-generated content, identify the model that produced it, or even the model creator. These capabilities are crucial for keeping trust in online communication platforms, for content moderation, and for making sure AI is deployed responsibly.

The motivation for this research comes from real-life scenarios, where we often do not know which specific model was used to generate a piece of text. We can formulate these scenarios as "Cross-Model Detection". Here we look at whether a classifier that was trained to distinguish text generated by one LM from human-written text can also identify text that was generated by a different LM, without fine-tuning or training on the text that this other LM produces.

What characterizes our contribution to this area is how comprehensive the study is. Previous works in the literature only explored a few model sizes and families, but we take a broader approach. We systematically look at a wide range of LLM sizes, from base models up to exceptionally large ones, and we cover diverse model families like GPT-2, LLaMA, Pythia, OPT and others. We also explore the impact of conversational fine-tuning techniques, including Chat, Instruct, and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), and the impact of model quantization and of watermarking the generated text, on how well the classifier generalizes and transfers across this wide array of models.

Because the investigation is so comprehensive, we get a deeper understanding of how the classifier generalizes and transfers across a diverse set of models, and this removes a potential source of bias in our results. It also lets us find out how the factors mentioned above (model size, family, conversational finetuning, quantization and watermarking) impact the detection and attribution of generated text.

Our contributions in this study are the following:

- A comprehensive investigation into cross-model detection, where we evaluate the classifier's ability to detect text generated by different LLMs, and into model attribution, covering a broad range of sizes and model families.

- We show the role of both model size and family in detecting text generated by LLMs. We see an inverse relationship between how effective the classifier is and the size of the LLM. Larger models can be hard to detect, but training on LLMs of similar size can improve performance. Our study also gives insights into the impact of conversational finetuning, quantization and watermarking on detection, and shows that LLM detection is robust to these techniques.

- Our model attribution experiments show that it is possible to identify the source model of generated text. Human-generated text can be distinguished, and the confusion happens mostly between models from the same family or with adjacent sizes. This suggests that LLMs leave distinct signatures, which makes it possible to identify the source model and classify the model family, and this improves our understanding of how different LLMs generate text.

In the next sections, we first summarize related work and then give the details of our methodology, experiments and results, which shed light on the interplay between model size, family and training data for LLM detection and attribution in the ever-evolving landscape of Large Language Models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs), known for their ability to generate human-like text [1], have found applications in various domains, including content generation, chatbots, and language translation. However, as LLMs become more widely used, concerns have surfaced about their misuse, misinformation, and ethical implications [2,3,4]. One way to address these concerns is through robust methods able to detect and attribute text generated by LLMs [5], allowing us to differentiate between human-authored and machine-generated content, identify the source model, or even the model creator. Such capabilities are crucial for maintaining trust in online communication platforms, for content moderation, and for ensuring responsible AI deployment.

Our motivation for this research comes from real-life scenarios in which we often lack knowledge of the specific model used to generate a piece of text. These scenarios can be formulated as "Cross-Model Detection", where we investigate whether a classifier originally trained to distinguish between text generated by one LM and human-written text can also identify text generated by a different LM, without fine-tuning or training on the text that LM produces.

Our contribution to this area lies in the comprehensiveness of our study. While previous works in the literature have explored only a few model sizes and families, we take a more expansive approach. We systematically examine a wide range of LLM sizes, from base models to exceptionally large ones, and cover diverse model families such as GPT-2, LLaMA, Pythia, OPT and others [6]. We also explore the impact of conversational fine-tuning techniques, including Chat, Instruct [7,8], and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [9,10], as well as the impact of model quantization and watermarking of the generated text, on the generalization and transferability of the classifier across this wide array of models.

This comprehensive investigation gives us a deeper understanding of the generalization and transferability of the classifier across a diverse array of models, eliminating a potential source of bias in our results. It also allows us to identify how the factors mentioned above (model size, family, conversational finetuning, quantization and watermarking) impact the detection and attribution of generated text.

Our contributions in this study can be summarized as follows:

- A comprehensive investigation into cross-model detection, evaluating the classifier's ability to detect text generated by different LLMs, and into model attribution, covering a broad range of sizes and model families.

- We highlight the role of both model size and family in detecting text generated by LLMs. We observe an inverse relationship between classifier effectiveness and LLM size: detecting larger models can be challenging, but training on similarly sized LLMs can improve performance. Our study also provides insights into the impact of conversational finetuning, quantization, and watermarking on detection, indicating that LLM detection is robust to these techniques.

- Our model attribution experiments show that the source model of generated text can be identified. While human-generated text is distinguishable, confusion occurs mainly between models from the same family or with adjacent sizes. This suggests that LLMs leave distinct signatures, which enable source model identification and model family classification and further our understanding of how different LLMs generate text.

In the following sections, we summarize relevant related work and then present the details of our methodology, experiments, and results, shedding light on the interplay between model size, family, and training data for LLM detection and attribution in the ever-evolving landscape of Large Language Models.
